title: All Saints Day in Poland: Znicze, Zaduszki and Candlelight
excerpt: All Saints Day in Poland explained: Wszystkich Świętych vs Zaduszki, znicze and chrysanthemums, the Powązki kwesta, Dziady roots and visitor etiquette.
metaDescription: All Saints Day in Poland explained: Wszystkich Świętych vs Zaduszki, znicze and chrysanthemums, the Powązki kwesta, Dziady roots and visitor etiquette.
summary: 1 November (Wszystkich Świętych) is a public holiday when Poles clean and decorate family graves; 2 November (Zaduszki) is All Souls' Day and a normal working day.
Znicze (candles in glass jars) and potted chrysanthemums turn Polish cemeteries into fields of light after dark.
Since 1975, volunteers at Warsaw's Stare Powązki cemetery have collected money each year to restore historic tombstones.
The holiday's roots reach back to the pre-Christian Slavic rite of dziady, which inspired Adam Mickiewicz's drama of the same name.

factNotes: Focus keyword 'all saints day poland' is grammatically awkward as an exact phrase; density (~1.0%) was reached with constructions like 'On All Saints Day Poland's...' and 'the All Saints Day Poland observes' (no apostrophe used in 'All Saints Day' for consistency with the keyword). Left out: number of travellers/visitors (no source), Akcja Znicz accident stats, chrysanthemum prices, total money raised by the Powązki kwesta (sources disagree; only the ~1,600 conservation works figure from 2023 PAP coverage is used), 'actors since decades' kept only for Maja Komorowska (verified). Hedged as general custom: lighting a candle on neglected graves ('some people'), not giving chrysanthemums as gifts ('many Poles'), special cemetery transport lines ('many cities'), dark clothing ('many people'). Removed an unsourced claim that jazz was frowned upon by authorities in 1954. Halloween section avoids any popularity statistics. 2027 weekdays (Mon 1 Nov, Tue 2 Nov) computed.
